theirs: Heavenly Father is a glorified, exalted being with 'a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's' (D&C 130:22), and He is the literal Father of every human spirit — all people lived with Him as His spirit children before birth (True to the Faith: Plan of Salvation). The Gospel Topics essay 'Becoming Like God' affirms Joseph Smith's teaching that God 'was once as one of us,' while noting that 'little has been revealed' about that and it is therefore little taught. Because we are His children in a full and complete sense, the faithful can grow to become like Him — receiving exaltation through Christ's Atonement — yet exalted beings 'will always worship' Heavenly Father (Gospel Topics essay: Becoming Like God).
bible: God is spirit, not flesh (John 4:24), eternal and unchanging — 'from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God' (Psalm 90:2; Malachi 3:6). He alone is and has ever been God: 'before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me' (Isaiah 43:10). Humans are His creatures made in His image (Genesis 1:27), loved and adopted as children through Christ, but never of the same order of being as their Creator.
key: Whether God is an embodied, exalted being of the same kind humanity can become, or an eternally unique spirit who alone has ever been God.

theirs: Jesus Christ is the Firstborn of the Father's spirit children, 'the Great Jehovah of the Old Testament, the Messiah of the New,' and the Only Begotten Son of the Father in the flesh (Gospel Topics: Jesus Christ; The Living Christ). Under the Father's direction He created the earth (John 1:3 as cited there). He suffered for the sins of the world in Gethsemane and on the cross, gave His life to atone for all mankind, and rose from the grave as 'the firstfruits of them that slept.' 'Only by His mercy and grace can anyone be saved,' and He is the only way back to Heavenly Father (Gospel Topics: Jesus Christ).
bible: Jesus is the eternal Word who 'was God' and through whom all things were made — He is uncreated (John 1:1–3). In Him 'dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily' (Colossians 2:9); He is the exact imprint of God's being who upholds the universe (Hebrews 1:3). Historic creeds confess Him as fully God and fully man, 'begotten, not made,' of one being with the Father — the crucified and risen Savior and only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).
key: Both confess Jesus as divine Savior and Redeemer; they differ on whether He is the uncreated God Himself, one in being with the Father, or the firstborn of the Father's spirit children — a distinct divine being.

theirs: The Godhead consists of three separate beings: God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost (Articles of Faith 1:1), who are perfectly 'one in purpose and doctrine' (Gospel Topics: Godhead). The Father and the Son have tangible bodies of flesh and bones, while 'the Holy Ghost has not a body of flesh and bones, but is a personage of Spirit' (D&C 130:22). The Holy Ghost testifies of the Father and the Son, comforts, sanctifies, and reveals 'the truth of all things' (Moroni 10:5), and the gift of the Holy Ghost — the right to His constant companionship — is conferred by the laying on of hands after baptism (Gospel Topics: Holy Ghost).
bible: There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), who exists eternally as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — sharing one divine being and name (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). The Spirit is a divine person, not a force: He teaches, intercedes, and can be grieved (John 14:26; Romans 8:26–27). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: not three gods united in purpose, but one God in three persons.
key: Three separate divine beings united in purpose versus one God existing eternally as three persons.

theirs: 'We believe the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly; we also believe the Book of Mormon to be the word of God' (Articles of Faith 1:8). The Bible witnesses of Christ, but 'is not, as it is currently available, without error,' since parts were altered or lost in transmission (Gospel Topics: Bible). The Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, and Pearl of Great Price clarify and corroborate the biblical witness, and the canon is open — 'God continues to reveal His word through living prophets today' (Gospel Topics: Bible; Articles of Faith 1:9).
bible: 'All scripture is given by inspiration of God' and thoroughly equips God's people (2 Timothy 3:16–17); 'the word of our God shall stand for ever' (Isaiah 40:8), reliably preserved. The faith was 'once delivered unto the saints' (Jude 3), founded on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Historic Christianity therefore holds the biblical canon closed and complete — the final rule by which every later claim to revelation is tested.
key: Whether God's written word is a closed, sufficient biblical canon or an open canon that living prophets continue to expand.

theirs: Heavenly Father's plan of salvation spans premortal life, mortality — where we gain a physical body and 'prove ourselves' — death, resurrection, and judgment (True to the Faith: Plan of Salvation). Through Christ's Atonement all people will be resurrected and saved from physical death, unconditionally; 'we believe that through the Atonement of Christ, all mankind may be saved, by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Gospel' (Articles of Faith 1:3). Eternal life, or exaltation — living forever in God's presence — comes through faith in Christ, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, and enduring to the end, and the glory one receives 'will depend on the depth of your conversion and your obedience to the Lord's commandments' (True to the Faith: Plan of Salvation; D&C 76:51).
bible: Salvation is God's rescue of sinners from sin and judgment into eternal life, accomplished entirely by Christ's death and resurrection (Romans 5:8–9). It is received as a gift: 'For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works' (Ephesians 2:8–9); 'he that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life' (John 3:36). The saved are brought into one shared destiny — dwelling with God forever — rather than graded levels of reward for obedience, though Scripture does speak of differing rewards within that one inheritance (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).
key: Salvation as a tiered plan — universal resurrection plus exaltation through ordinances and obedience — versus a single rescue from sin received through faith in Christ.

theirs: Grace is 'the divine help or strength extended to us through the Atonement of the Lord Jesus Christ' — an enabling power that strengthens us to do what we could not do on our own (Gospel Topics: Grace). Through grace all will be resurrected, and those who obey the gospel — faith, repentance, baptism, receiving the Holy Ghost, and striving to follow Christ throughout life — can be forgiven and made clean (Gospel Topics: Grace; Articles of Faith 1:4). As Nephi taught, 'it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do' (2 Nephi 25:23) — grace and faithful discipleship work together, never in isolation (cf. James 2:17–22 as cited there).
bible: A person is 'justified by faith without the deeds of the law' (Romans 3:28); salvation is 'not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy' (Titus 3:5). Good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of genuine faith — 'faith without works is dead' (James 2:26) — but they flow from salvation rather than completing it: we are 'created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Ephesians 2:10), not saved by them.
key: Whether grace saves apart from works — with works as the fruit — or grace enables and works with required ordinances and obedience to bring full salvation.

theirs: The Fall of Adam and Eve 'is an integral part of Heavenly Father's plan of salvation' — a step 'downward yet forward' that made mortality, posterity, and progression possible (Gospel Topics: Fall of Adam and Eve). 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy' (2 Nephi 2:25). The Fall brought physical and spiritual death and a fallen condition we all inherit, but 'men will be punished for their own sins, and not for Adam's transgression' (Articles of Faith 1:2) — there is no original guilt, and little children are innocent and 'alive in Christ' (Moroni 8:12, 22).
bible: The Fall was a catastrophic act of rebellion: 'by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men' (Romans 5:12). Humanity is now sinful by nature, not merely by choice — 'in sin did my mother conceive me' (Psalm 51:5) — 'dead in trespasses and sins' and unable to save itself (Ephesians 2:1–5). The Fall is the disaster the gospel remedies, answered by the obedience of the second Adam, Christ (Romans 5:18–19).
key: Whether the Fall was a planned, necessary step forward in God's plan or a catastrophic rebellion that left human nature corrupted and helpless apart from rescue.

theirs: At death spirits enter the spirit world — paradise or spirit prison — where the gospel is preached to the dead, who may accept ordinances such as baptism performed on their behalf in temples (Gospel Topics: Temples; D&C 138). After resurrection and judgment, nearly everyone inherits one of three kingdoms of glory: the celestial kingdom, where the faithful dwell with the Father and the Son; the terrestrial, for honorable people 'who were blinded by the craftiness of men'; and the telestial, for those who 'received not the gospel of Christ, neither the testimony of Jesus' (D&C 76; Gospel Topics: Kingdoms of Glory). Only the sons of perdition, who fully knew and then denied God's power, are cast into outer darkness (D&C 76:31–37).
bible: Scripture presents two final destinies: 'these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal' (Matthew 25:46); all will rise 'they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation' (John 5:28–29). 'It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment' (Hebrews 9:27) — one's standing with God is fixed in this life. The redeemed dwell with God in a new heaven and new earth (Revelation 21:1–4).
key: Three graded kingdoms of glory with opportunity to receive the gospel after death, versus two final destinies settled by one's response to Christ in this life.

theirs: Resurrection is assured to all through Christ, but eternal life is a covenant path walked to its end: 'if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life' (D&C 14:7). Disciples 'press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope' (2 Nephi 31:20), and the Holy Ghost gives peace and assurance as they keep their covenants. The Holy Spirit of Promise confirms that ordinances and covenants are 'acceptable to God,' contingent on continued faithfulness (Gospel Topics: Holy Ghost) — so confidence is real, but final judgment rests with a perfectly merciful and just Lord.
bible: 'These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life' (1 John 5:13) — assurance is presented as present-tense knowledge. Jesus said His sheep 'shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand' (John 10:28), and 'there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus' (Romans 8:1). Because assurance rests on Christ's finished work rather than the believer's performance, nothing 'shall be able to separate us from the love of God' (Romans 8:38–39).
key: Whether a believer can presently know they have eternal life on the basis of Christ's finished work, or must faithfully endure to the end to receive it.

theirs: God guides His Church today as anciently — through living prophets. Members sustain the President of the Church as 'prophet, seer, and revelator — the only person on the earth who receives revelation to guide the entire Church' (Gospel Topics: Prophets). The prophet's inspired word carries the Lord's own authority — 'whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same' (D&C 1:38) — and heeding it brings the promise that 'the gates of hell shall not prevail against you' (D&C 21:4–6). Every member may also receive personal revelation through the Holy Ghost for their own life and stewardship.
bible: God, who spoke 'at sundry times and in divers manners… by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son' (Hebrews 1:1–2) — Christ is God's final and fullest word. The church is 'built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets,' a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20). All later claims to speak for God must be tested against that apostolic gospel: 'though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel… let him be accursed' (Galatians 1:8; cf. Deuteronomy 18:20–22).
key: Whether God leads His people today through a living prophet with binding new revelation, or has spoken definitively in Christ and the once-laid apostolic witness of Scripture.

theirs: After the deaths of Christ's Apostles, 'men corrupted the principles of the gospel and made unauthorized changes in Church organization and priesthood ordinances,' and the Lord 'withdrew the authority of the priesthood from the earth' — the Great Apostasy (True to the Faith: Apostasy). What was lost could not be reformed; it had to be restored: God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to Joseph Smith in 1820, and priesthood authority and keys were restored through heavenly messengers (Gospel Topics: Restoration of the Priesthood). The Lord declared the restored Church 'the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth' (D&C 1:30), organized 'the same organization that existed in the Primitive Church' with apostles, prophets, and ordinances (Articles of Faith 1:6).
bible: Jesus promised, 'I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it' (Matthew 16:18), and pledged His presence 'alway, even unto the end of the world' (Matthew 28:20) — historic Christianity therefore denies any total apostasy. The church is not one institution's exclusive franchise but the whole body of those in Christ, 'one body' baptized by one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13), built on the apostles' foundation with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–22).
key: Whether Christ's church and priesthood authority vanished from the earth and required restoration through Joseph Smith, or have continued unbroken among Christ's people since the apostles.

theirs: 'Marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God and… the family is central to the Creator's plan for the eternal destiny of His children' (The Family: A Proclamation to the World). Gender is 'an essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose' (Proclamation). When a couple is sealed in the temple, their marriage endures beyond death — 'the new and everlasting covenant of marriage' is required to obtain the highest degree of the celestial kingdom (D&C 131:1–4), and children sealed to parents make 'it possible for families to be united eternally' (Proclamation; Gospel Topics: Temples).
bible: Marriage is God's good creation ordinance — 'they twain shall be one flesh' (Genesis 2:24) — and a living picture of Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Yet it belongs to this age: 'in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven' (Matthew 22:30). The everlasting family is God's household of the redeemed — 'whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother' (Mark 3:35).
key: Whether marriage and family are eternal and essential to the highest salvation, or temporal gifts whose picture is fulfilled in Christ's eternal union with His people.

theirs: Temples are 'houses of the Lord' where sacred ordinances are performed: the endowment — 'instructions and covenants to live righteously' centered on the Savior — celestial marriage sealing husband and wife for eternity, and baptism and other ordinances performed on behalf of the dead (Gospel Topics: Temples). These ordinances are 'necessary for the children of God to enable them to return to dwell with Him.' Entry requires worthiness and a temple recommend from priesthood leaders, and all the Church's activity ultimately 'leads to the work done in holy temples' (Gospel Topics: Temples). Weekly worship, including the sacrament, takes place in local meetinghouses open to all.
bible: Christ's once-for-all sacrifice fulfilled and ended the temple system: 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (Hebrews 10:14), and the veil was torn, giving every believer 'boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus' (Hebrews 10:19–20). God's temple is now His people — 'ye are the temple of God' (1 Corinthians 3:16) — and true worship is bound to no sacred site: 'in spirit and in truth' (John 4:21–24). No further rites are needed to gain access to God beyond faith in the finished work of Christ.
key: Whether saving ordinances performed in temples are required to return to God's presence, or Christ's finished sacrifice opened direct access and ended the need for temple rites.

theirs: Jesus Christ will return 'in power and glory to claim the earth as His kingdom' — a day of peace for the righteous — though 'the hour and the day no man knoweth' (Gospel Topics: Second Coming of Jesus Christ; D&C 49:7). Prophesied signs include the Restoration of the gospel and priesthood keys, the coming forth of the Book of Mormon, and the gospel preached throughout the world (Gospel Topics: Second Coming). 'Christ will reign personally upon the earth' during the Millennium, 'Zion (the New Jerusalem) will be built upon the American continent,' and 'the earth will be renewed and receive its paradisiacal glory' (Articles of Faith 1:10).
bible: 'This same Jesus… shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven' (Acts 1:11) — a visible, bodily return at an hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36). The dead will rise, all will stand before God's judgment (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 20:11–15), and God will dwell with His people in a new heaven and new earth where 'there shall be no more death' (Revelation 21:1–4). Christians hold differing views on the millennium's nature, but agree on one climactic return, final judgment, and eternal state.
key: Both await Christ's literal return; the distinctives are the Restoration and Book of Mormon as prophesied latter-day signs and a New Jerusalem to be built on the American continent.
